title: Epilogue
html:
Shortly after Baodium introduced personalized recommendations, customers began waiting longer for product pages that had previously loaded without difficulty. The new feature passed its functional checks, and its database queries were still fast. The problem was the additional work each request created. At production traffic, recommendation lookups occupied enough connections that other requests began waiting for the shared pool.

The engineers found the cause by measuring how often queries acquired a connection, how long they waited, and how long they used it. Those measurements gave the team a way to evaluate the next release. They also led to a product decision: if recommendations could not finish within their allowance, the page could return without them. The choice depended on what the customer needed from the page and what the application could safely omit.

Later incidents asked different questions. When a payment response was lost, the engineers needed a record that distinguished an unknown outcome from a failed one. When fraud evaluation slowed, they needed to limit work entering the dependency before waiting requests consumed the available workers. When a replica returned an older address after an update, they needed to decide how fresh that particular read had to be. The useful measurements and recovery procedures differed, because the customer promises differed.

By the European launch, these decisions had become connected. Capacity reserved for new payment authorizations could not also be allocated to reconciliation. A surviving region could not begin writing an account’s payment history until it had established ownership and understood the operations missing from its replica. A deployment could pass its health checks while increasing database work for every product-page request. The review had to account for those effects together, then test the failure procedures with the engineers who would use them.

Another application will need a different arrangement. A document service may accept a file, return a status reference, and finish indexing it later. A booking system may have to prevent two customers from reserving the same seat. An internal change-validation service may need to refuse a deployment that was approved under an earlier policy revision. In each case, we can begin with the operation the customer or caller expects to complete, identify who owns its authoritative state, and establish what recovery will do if execution stops halfway through.

The Hidden Assumptions reviews provide a record of the decisions made along the way. A pool calculation needs revisiting when a request begins making more queries. A recovery procedure needs another rehearsal when a provider changes its retry or status-lookup contract. A capacity estimate borrowed from another region needs replacing with local measurements. Keeping those assumptions visible gives the next engineer something useful to examine when production behavior changes.

I began this book with engineers gathering around a whiteboard. We will still need the boxes and arrows. They help us see where requests go and which components depend on one another. As the drawing develops, we can also ask what each operation promises, how much work it creates, what survives an interruption, and which evidence would make us revise the design. Those are conversations worth having while the system is still on the whiteboard, and worth returning to long after it reaches production.
